blocks.text: A 58-year-old man with advanced liver cirrhosis has a plasma albumin of 22 g/L (well below the typical reference range, which varies by laboratory). His ankles are swollen and his abdomen is distended with free fluid. His heart and capillary pressures are normal, yet fluid is escaping from his circulation. The forces that govern this escape were described by Ernest Starling.

blocks.markdown: The **microcirculation** is the network of arterioles, capillaries and venules where blood and tissue exchange materials. Capillary walls are a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, with narrow clefts between cells. Lipid-soluble substances and gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide) cross by **simple diffusion**, the main route of exchange. Water and small solutes also cross through the intercellular clefts, and the movement of *fluid* itself is driven by the balance of hydrostatic and osmotic pressures, called **bulk flow**. Plasma proteins, which are too large to leave readily, stay in the vessels and exert an osmotic pull.

blocks.title: Starling forces
blocks.text: Four pressures determine net fluid movement across a capillary wall: capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) and interstitial oncotic pressure (πi) tend to push fluid out; interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi) and plasma (capillary) oncotic pressure (πc) tend to hold fluid in. Oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure is the osmotic pressure generated by proteins, chiefly albumin, which cannot cross the wall freely. Net filtration is the sum of these opposing forces.

blocks.caption: Starling equation: Jv is net fluid movement out of the capillary (positive = filtration); Kf is the filtration coefficient (water permeability times surface area); sigma is the reflection coefficient of the proteins (close to 1 when the wall is impermeable to them, so it is taken as 1 here).

rows: About 35 at the arteriolar end, falling to about 15 at the venular end
Close to zero (slightly sub-atmospheric in some tissues)
Small, a few mmHg at most
blocks.caption: The four Starling forces. Values are illustrative teaching figures; real values differ between tissues and between textbooks.

blocks.title: Net filtration pressure along a capillary
blocks.prompt: Take Pc = 35 mmHg at the arteriolar end and 15 mmHg at the venular end, with plasma oncotic pressure 25 mmHg, and treat Pi and πi as zero. Calculate the net filtration pressure at each end.

steps.text: Net filtration pressure is the outward hydrostatic pressure minus the inward oncotic pressure (with Pi and πi taken as zero).

blocks.answer: Fluid is filtered out (+10 mmHg) at the arteriolar end and, in this simplified model, drawn back in (-10 mmHg) at the venular end. In reality the capillary overall filters slightly more than it reabsorbs, and the excess is returned by lymphatics.

blocks.markdown: **Raised venous pressure.** Pressure in the veins is transmitted backwards to the capillaries, and because the resistance of the postcapillary side is low, a rise in venous pressure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure much more effectively than a similar rise in arterial pressure, which is buffered by the arterioles. Higher Pc increases filtration and reduces reabsorption. This occurs in right heart failure (systemic venous congestion), in deep vein thrombosis (local venous obstruction) and in prolonged standing.

blocks.title: Effect of low plasma albumin
blocks.prompt: A patient with malnutrition has plasma oncotic pressure reduced from 25 mmHg to 15 mmHg. Pc is unchanged (35 mmHg arteriolar end, 15 mmHg venular end), and Pi and πi are taken as zero. Calculate the net filtration pressure at each end and state what has changed.

steps.text: Compared with normal (+10 and -10), filtration at the arteriolar end has doubled and the inward force that normally draws fluid back at the venular end has disappeared.

blocks.answer: NFP is +20 mmHg at the arteriolar end and 0 mmHg at the venular end. More fluid is filtered and none is reabsorbed, so interstitial fluid accumulates (oedema) unless the lymphatics can carry the extra.

blocks.title: Net filtration is outward; lymph returns the excess
blocks.text: Averaged over the whole capillary bed, slightly more fluid leaves than returns. The remainder, together with any protein that leaks out, is returned to the circulation by the lymphatic system (typically a few litres per day). Oedema develops when filtration exceeds the capacity of the lymphatics to drain the interstitium.

blocks.markdown: **The lymphatic system** begins as blind-ended **lymphatic capillaries** in the interstitium. Their endothelial cells overlap like flaps and are tethered by anchoring filaments, so that when the interstitial space swells the flaps open and fluid, protein and cells can enter, but cannot leave. Lymph then flows through progressively larger vessels containing valves that ensure one-way flow, passes through lymph nodes, and is finally returned to the venous system via the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct near the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins.

items: Lymph is propelled by intrinsic contraction of smooth muscle in lymph vessel walls and by external compression from skeletal muscle contraction, arterial pulsation and breathing, with valves preventing backflow.
Lymphatics return filtered fluid to the blood, which maintains plasma volume.
They return plasma proteins that have leaked into the interstitium, which could not otherwise get back (protein is a main driver of interstitial oncotic pressure).
Lymph nodes filter lymph and support immune surveillance.
Lymph flow can increase many-fold when interstitial pressure rises, a major safety factor against oedema.

rows: Right heart failure; deep vein thrombosis; prolonged standing
Sigma falls and protein leaks, reducing the net oncotic gradient
Inflammation or allergic reactions (for example histamine release)
Drainage fails and protein accumulates in the interstitium
Surgical removal of lymph nodes; parasitic filarial infection
blocks.caption: Causes of oedema and the Starling term each alters.

blocks.title: Illustrative numbers, not constants
blocks.text: The values used in teaching vary by tissue: the liver and glomerulus have very different permeability and pressures from skeletal muscle. Modern descriptions of the Starling principle also stress that reabsorption of fluid at the venular end is much smaller than the classical picture suggests, and that lymphatic return is correspondingly more important. Use the equation for direction and relative size of effects.

points: Net fluid movement across capillaries follows the Starling equation: Jv = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - sigma x (πc - πi)]; Pc and πi favour filtration, πc and Pi oppose it.
Raised venous pressure raises Pc and low plasma albumin lowers πc; each increases filtration and can cause oedema.
Lymphatics return the excess filtered fluid and leaked protein to the venous circulation and increase their flow when more fluid is filtered.
Oedema arises when filtration exceeds lymphatic drainage: from higher Pc, lower πc, higher permeability or lymphatic obstruction.

questions.stem: Which Starling force is the main driver of fluid filtration out of a capillary?

options.text: Plasma oncotic pressure
Capillary hydrostatic pressure
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure
The reflection coefficient

distractorRationale.a: Plasma oncotic pressure draws fluid into the capillary, opposing filtration.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out through the wall.
distractorRationale.c: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure is close to zero and opposes filtration.
distractorRationale.d: The reflection coefficient is a property of the wall describing protein permeability, not a force.

questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure of blood within the capillary pushes fluid outwards, and it is the dominant outward force. The plasma oncotic pressure, produced mainly by albumin, acts in the opposite direction.

questions.stem: Which statement about plasma oncotic pressure is correct?

options.text: It is generated mainly by plasma sodium and favours filtration out of the capillary
It is generated mainly by plasma proteins, chiefly albumin, and draws fluid into the capillary
It is generated by red blood cells and is equal to the capillary hydrostatic pressure
It is generated by lymph and moves fluid out of the interstitium into cells

questions.correctOptionText: It is generated mainly by plasma proteins, chiefly albumin, and draws fluid into the capillary

distractorRationale.a: Sodium crosses the capillary wall freely, so it does not generate a sustained osmotic force across it.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: proteins cannot cross the wall readily, so their oncotic pressure pulls fluid into the capillary.
distractorRationale.c: Red cells are not responsible, and there is no equality with hydrostatic pressure.
distractorRationale.d: Lymph does not generate oncotic pressure moving fluid into cells.

questions.explanation: Oncotic pressure is the osmotic pressure caused by macromolecules that cannot cross the capillary wall, mostly albumin. It acts in the direction of drawing fluid from the interstitium into the plasma, opposing the outward hydrostatic push.

questions.stem: At one point along a skeletal muscle capillary the capillary hydrostatic pressure is 30 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure is 2 mmHg, plasma oncotic pressure is 25 mmHg and interstitial oncotic pressure is 3 mmHg. Taking the reflection coefficient as 1, calculate the net filtration pressure in mmHg (positive means net movement out of the capillary).
questions.explanation: Net pressure is (Pc - Pi) - (πc - πi) = (30 - 2) - (25 - 3) = 28 - 22 = +6 mmHg. The positive sign means there is net filtration out of the capillary at this point.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman returns from a long-haul flight with a swollen, tender left calf. Ultrasound shows a thrombus in a deep leg vein. Her right leg and plasma albumin are normal. Which change in the Starling forces best explains the swelling of the left calf?

options.text: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure from venous obstruction, increasing filtration
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from low albumin
Raised plasma oncotic pressure drawing fluid into the leg
Reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure from arteriolar dilation

questions.correctOptionText: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure from venous obstruction, increasing filtration

distractorRationale.a: Correct: obstructed outflow raises venous pressure, which is transmitted back to the capillaries and raises Pc.
distractorRationale.b: Plasma albumin is stated to be normal, and a systemic change would not affect only one leg.
distractorRationale.c: A higher plasma oncotic pressure would oppose filtration, not cause swelling.
distractorRationale.d: A lower Pc would reduce filtration, the opposite of the findings.

questions.explanation: A thrombus in the deep vein obstructs venous return from that leg, raising venous pressure behind the block. The rise is transmitted back to the capillaries, increasing Pc, filtration and interstitial fluid until lymphatic drainage cannot keep up, and the swelling is limited to the affected leg.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with severe malnutrition has a swollen abdomen and ankle oedema. Plasma oncotic pressure has fallen to 12 mmHg. At the venular end of the capillary the hydrostatic pressure is 15 mmHg. Treating interstitial pressures as zero, calculate the net filtration pressure at the venular end in mmHg (positive means net movement out of the capillary).
questions.explanation: Net filtration pressure is Pc - πc = 15 - 12 = +3 mmHg. In health this value is negative (about 15 - 25 = -10 mmHg in the illustrative model), so fluid is normally drawn back in at the venular end; in hypoalbuminaemia it becomes positive, so fluid continues to leave and oedema develops.

questions.stem: What is the principal function of the lymphatic system in relation to tissue fluid?

options.text: To generate plasma oncotic pressure
To return filtered interstitial fluid and leaked protein to the venous circulation
To deliver oxygen to tissues
To raise capillary hydrostatic pressure

questions.correctOptionText: To return filtered interstitial fluid and leaked protein to the venous circulation

distractorRationale.a: Oncotic pressure is generated by plasma proteins, not by the lymphatic system.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: lymphatics drain excess interstitial fluid and protein back to the blood.
distractorRationale.c: Oxygen is delivered by blood capillaries, not by lymph.
distractorRationale.d: Lymphatics tend to reduce interstitial fluid, not raise capillary pressure.

questions.explanation: Slightly more fluid is filtered than reabsorbed, and plasma proteins also leak out. Lymphatics collect this fluid and protein and return it to the veins, preventing oedema and protecting plasma volume.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman develops a persistently swollen right arm some months after surgical clearance of her axillary lymph nodes. Pulses, venous pressure and plasma albumin are normal. What is the mechanism of the swelling?

options.text: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure in the arm
Impaired lymphatic drainage, so filtered fluid and protein accumulate in the interstitium
Raised venous pressure from right heart failure
Excessive reabsorption of fluid at the venular end

questions.correctOptionText: Impaired lymphatic drainage, so filtered fluid and protein accumulate in the interstitium

distractorRationale.a: Plasma albumin is normal and a systemic oncotic change would not be confined to one arm.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: removing nodes disrupts lymph flow, so normal filtration is no longer matched by drainage.
distractorRationale.c: Venous pressure is stated to be normal and heart failure would cause generalised swelling.
distractorRationale.d: Excessive reabsorption would reduce, not increase, interstitial fluid.

questions.explanation: Normal capillary filtration produces a small net excess of interstitial fluid and protein that the lymphatics remove. If lymphatic drainage is damaged, the fluid and protein accumulate in the tissue drained by those vessels and the arm swells.

questions.stem: In a localised bacterial skin infection (cellulitis), a red swollen area develops after histamine and other mediators increase capillary permeability to proteins. Which change in the Starling balance best explains the tissue swelling?

options.text: Plasma proteins leak into the interstitium, reducing the effective oncotic gradient that holds fluid in the capillary and raising filtration
Plasma oncotic pressure rises because water is lost from the plasma
Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls, drawing fluid into the tissue
Lymphatic vessels lose all function in the infected area

questions.correctOptionText: Plasma proteins leak into the interstitium, reducing the effective oncotic gradient that holds fluid in the capillary and raising filtration

distractorRationale.a: Correct: leakier walls lower the reflection coefficient and let protein out, reducing the net oncotic gradient.
distractorRationale.b: A rising plasma oncotic pressure would oppose filtration, not cause swelling.
distractorRationale.c: A fall in Pc would reduce filtration; in inflammation the local arterioles dilate and Pc usually rises.
distractorRationale.d: Lymph function is not lost entirely; the swelling reflects excess filtration.

questions.explanation: Mediators such as histamine open the endothelial clefts, lowering the reflection coefficient so that proteins leak out. The oncotic pressure difference that normally holds fluid in is diminished, and with arteriolar dilation raising Pc, filtration increases and the tissue swells.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with right-sided heart failure has swollen ankles. Using the Starling equation, explain how his condition produces oedema, and contrast this mechanism with that of oedema from low plasma albumin.
markingGuide: States the Starling equation or the four forces: Pc and πi out, πc and Pi in
Right heart failure raises central venous pressure, which backs up into systemic veins and is transmitted to capillaries
Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) therefore rises, so filtration increases and reabsorption decreases
When filtration exceeds lymphatic drainage, interstitial fluid accumulates, particularly in dependent areas such as the ankles because of gravity
Contrast: in low albumin, plasma oncotic pressure (πc) falls, so the inward force decreases, with Pc normal
Notes that both mechanisms increase net filtration and are limited only by lymphatic drainage capacity
questions.explanation: In heart failure the venous pressure rises, so Pc rises and pushes more fluid out of the capillary. In hypoalbuminaemia Pc is normal but πc falls, so the inward force is weakened; both disturb the balance in favour of filtration and cause oedema once lymphatic return is exceeded.

questions.stem: Describe how the lymphatic system returns interstitial fluid to the circulation, and explain why it acts as a safety factor against oedema.
markingGuide: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended with overlapping endothelial flaps that open to let fluid, protein and cells in
Fluid enters when interstitial pressure rises, and cannot flow back out
Lymph moves through vessels with valves, propelled by smooth muscle contraction and by compression from skeletal muscle and breathing
Lymph passes through lymph nodes and returns to the venous system via the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct
Also returns leaked plasma protein to the blood
Safety factor: lymph flow increases markedly when more fluid is filtered or interstitial pressure rises, so oedema occurs only when this capacity is exceeded
questions.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries take up the excess filtered fluid and protein through one-way endothelial flaps, and valved vessels carry it to the veins. Because lymph flow rises as interstitial fluid accumulates, the system buffers increases in filtration and oedema appears only when that capacity is overwhelmed.
